demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
become overly compliant when feeling threatened
Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't rely on other people
I can no longer trust my own body
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: 'Talks or photos about snakes' is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another unless the accident specifically involved a snake, which is not suggested anywhere else in the profile. The other trigger items point to generic post-traumatic cueing, but this item implies a highly specific trauma cue that lacks support from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: 'I was betrayed by someone I trusted' does not fit well with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another and is not supported by the other nodes. The profile otherwise centers on guilt, danger scanning, intrusive recollection, and distrust of self/body; betrayal by another person introduces a different interpersonal trauma theme without corroboration.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: Avoiding emotional closeness/intimacy is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The dominant threat and memory items concern danger, hypervigilance, intrusive imagery, numbness, and grief after an accidental injury event. Intimacy avoidance could occur, but here it appears to address an interpersonal/betrayal theme that is not otherwise coherently represented, especially given the unsupported betrayal appraisal.

issues.item: Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: The threat profile is dominated by generalized interpersonal/environmental danger monitoring (avoiding unfamiliar places, scanning exits in any room), which fits assault or deliberate threat contexts better than accidentally causing serious injury to another in an accident. For this trauma type, threat is more plausibly focused on accidents, loss of control, or harm recurrence rather than pervasive escape-oriented vigilance across all settings.

issues.item: Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'I can't rely on other people' is weakly grounded in the rest of the profile. The other nodes center on accident-related triggers, guilt, bodily unreliability, and generalized hypervigilance, but there is no corresponding interpersonal betrayal, abandonment, or dependence theme to support this item. It stands out as clinically disconnected from the trauma narrative and the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
Mei Lin was nineteen when she accidentally caused serious injury to another person. Driving home from the hair salon where she worked, a pedestrian darted into the crosswalk just as the light changed. She slammed the brakes, but the car slid; she heard the thud and saw the body crumple. The image of that moment-the figure appearing, the impact, the stillness afterward-became burned into her memory as vivid, recurring pictures. She later learned the victim survived but with lasting damage, and the weight of having failed to protect that person, of trusting a body that could not react in time, settled into a core belief: she could not rely on herself or anyone else.

In the weeks that followed, Mei began avoiding driving. The thought of getting behind the wheel triggered intrusive thoughts and vivid recall, so she relied on her boyfriend for rides or took the bus, even if it meant arriving late. At work in the salon, the sharp sound of a hair dryer or the clatter of scissors would make her jump-loud noises now felt like threats. That sense of threat kept the memory close, so that even in quiet moments the image of the pedestrian appearing just before impact would surface, unbidden and fully formed. She would scan the room for exits immediately upon entering any space, unable to relax even in the familiar salon. When a customer made an unexpected comment about driving or accidents, her heart would race and she would become overly compliant, agreeing with everything and apologizing excessively, a fawn response that left her feeling hollow. Her compliant behavior only deepened her belief that she was weak and unreliable; each time she fawned, she felt more certain that she could not stand up for herself. By avoiding driving, she never habituated, so any unexpected car noise became even more triggering, and her fear of driving grew stronger, making the world feel more dangerous.

As months passed, Mei found herself avoiding the anniversary of the accident. She arranged to work a double shift that day, hoping to distract herself. But the effort of keeping the memory at a distance had paradoxically kept it close-she had thought about not thinking about it every single shift, so when the anniversary finally arrived, the images came back with a force that felt magnified by all the weeks she had tried to suppress them. But even with the salon's constant activity, the date itself brought back the memory with overwhelming grief-she would remember the victim's family, the guilt, and sometimes she would recall the event but feel completely numb, as if it happened to someone else. The conviction that she had failed to protect that person made the memory resurface with an overwhelming sense of grief, and that emotionless blankness frightened her most, because it made her wonder if she had lost something essential. Her boyfriend tried to support her, but she distanced herself, convinced she could not rely on him either.

The causal loops tightened. Every time Mei heard a loud noise-a car backfiring outside the salon-her body reacted with a surge of adrenaline, and the intrusive images of the crash would flash before her eyes. That physical reactivity reaffirmed her belief that her own body was unreliable, that it betrayed her. Because she believed her own body was untrustworthy, she started to interpret any sudden sensation-a racing heart, a flinch-as a sign that something terrible was about to happen, making those sensations themselves become triggers. She would then scan the salon for exits, unable to concentrate, which only made her more certain she could not trust herself. Unable to relax, she found that her mind would drift back to the accident, the images surfacing without warning. The threat she perceived in safe places convinced her that danger was constant, which in turn made her hypervigilant to any possible reminders. She began to avoid any conversation about cars or accidents, and if a customer mentioned a recent collision, Mei would fawn again-nodding, apologizing, offering free services-to defuse what felt like an imminent confrontation.

Her relationship suffered. She canceled plans to avoid driving anywhere near the accident site. When her boyfriend pressed her, she became compliant and said everything was fine, but internally she felt alone. At the salon, her boss noticed she was jumpy and distracted, but Mei just apologized and worked harder, trying to please everyone.

What brought Mei to seek help was a moment at work when a customer suddenly dropped a metal tray; the crash sent Mei into a full panic-she dropped to her knees, shaking, and could not stop crying. She knew then that she could not keep living this way. She feared that if she did not get help, she would lose her job and her relationship. What frightened her most was the possibility that she would never feel safe again, that her body would always betray her, that she would always be responsible for the injury she caused. Yet she also hoped that someone could show her how to trust herself again.
